title: The New York Fed DSGE Model Forecast—September 2026 - Liberty Street Economics
gist: The New York Fed's DSGE model's September 2026 run keeps 2026 GDP growth at 1.2 percent but cuts 2027-2029 growth to 0.1/0.5/1.2 percent on lower TFP and more restrictive assumed policy, while raising the core PCE inflation path to 3.3/2.1/1.8/1.8 percent for 2026-2029. The model concedes it is again likely to be surprised to the upside on near-term growth, attributing the miss to buoyant financial conditions and an AI-related investment boom captured through marginal-efficiency-of-investment shocks.

insights.claim: The New York Fed DSGE model holds its 2026 Q4/Q4 GDP growth forecast at 1.2 percent, unchanged from its June 2026 run.
insights.speaker: peterstevens
insights.so_what: An unchanged current-year anchor means the entire story of this forecast round is in the out-years and the inflation path, not in 2026 activity.
insights.quote: The model’s growth forecasts for 2026 remained at 1.2 percent, as in June.
insights.locator: The model remains pessimistic on growth

insights.claim: GDP growth projections for 2027, 2028, and 2029 were cut to 0.1, 0.5, and 1.2 percent from 0.2, 0.7, and 1.5 percent three months earlier — a downgrade at every horizon.
insights.speaker: peterstevens
insights.so_what: A model-implied near-stall in 2027 (0.1 percent) is a tail-risk scenario worth pricing in rates and cyclical equity exposure, even if consensus is far above it.
insights.quote: The GDP growth projections for 2027, 2028, and 2029 are 0.1, 0.5, and 1.2 percent, respectively, compared to 0.2, 0.7, and 1.5 in June.
insights.locator: The GDP growth projections for 2027

insights.claim: Two explicit mechanisms drive the out-year growth downgrade: the model now expects monetary policy to be more restrictive than it assumed in June, and it revised down its expectations for total factor productivity growth.
insights.speaker: peterstevens
insights.so_what: The growth cut is a policy-plus-supply-side story, not a demand-shock story, so it does not mechanically imply a dovish Fed reaction function.
insights.quote: in part because the model expects monetary policy to be more restrictive than it did in June, and in part because it revised downward its expectations for total factor productivity (TFP) growth
insights.locator: The DSGE forecasts remain rather pessimistic on growth

insights.claim: The 68 percent uncertainty band around the 2026 GDP growth forecast narrowed sharply, from -2.2 to 4.5 percent in June down to -0.8 to 3.1 percent in September.
insights.speaker: peterstevens
insights.so_what: Narrowing near-term bands mean the model sees less macro ambiguity for the current year, which argues against paying up for very wide-strike macro optionality on 2026 activity.
insights.locator: Forecast Comparison table, GDP growth (Q4/Q4) row

insights.claim: Out-year GDP growth bands remain enormous — roughly -5.2 to 5.5 percent for 2027 and -4.4 to 6.8 percent for 2029 at just 68 percent confidence — so the point forecasts carry almost no discriminating power beyond one year.
insights.speaker: peterstevens
insights.so_what: Treat the headline out-year numbers as directional model signal, not as a tradable level; the honest read is that the model cannot distinguish boom from recession past 2027.
insights.locator: Forecast Comparison table, Notes: the numbers in parentheses are the 68 percent bands

insights.claim: The model's authors state outright that it remains pessimistic on growth and keeps being surprised when the economy turns out stronger than it expected — a rare explicit admission of systematic one-sided forecast error.
insights.speaker: peterstevens
insights.so_what: If the model has a known upside bias, fading its pessimistic growth track has been the profitable trade, and its out-year cuts should be discounted accordingly.
insights.quote: The model remains pessimistic on growth, and keeps being surprised when the economy turns out to be stronger than it expected.
insights.locator: The model remains pessimistic on growth

insights.claim: The Survey of Professional Forecasters puts 2026:Q3 GDP growth more than 1 percentage point higher in annualized terms than the DSGE model projected back in June, implying a large near-term forecast miss.
insights.speaker: peterstevens
insights.so_what: A greater-than-1-point gap between a structural model and professional forecasters in a single quarter is a live divergence to watch when Q3 data lands.
insights.quote: the SPF projects GDP growth in 2026:Q3 to be more than 1 percent higher in annualized terms than the DSGE model expected in June
insights.locator: In particular, the SPF projects GDP growth

insights.claim: The model decomposes its likely Q3 growth miss into two identified sources: more buoyant financial conditions than expected, and the positive growth effect of the AI-related boom in investment.
insights.speaker: peterstevens
insights.so_what: A Fed structural model formally attributing growth upside to AI capex and easy financial conditions validates those as the marginal macro drivers — and flags both as the things that would reverse the surprise if they roll over.
insights.quote: to more buoyant financial conditions than expected and to the positive growth effect of the AI-related boom in investment, as captured by MEI (marginal efficiency of investment) shocks
insights.locator: The model attributes this likely forecast miss

insights.claim: The AI investment boom enters the model only as marginal efficiency of investment (MEI) shocks — residuals — rather than as structural productivity, which is why higher AI capex lifts near-term growth without lifting the model's TFP path.
insights.speaker: peterstevens
insights.so_what: The internal contradiction — AI boosting growth via shocks while TFP is revised down — is exactly the debate on whether AI capex converts to measured productivity; the model currently says no.
insights.locator: as captured by MEI (marginal efficiency of investment) shocks

insights.claim: Core PCE inflation is now projected at 3.3, 2.1, 1.8, and 1.8 percent for 2026 through 2029, revised up from 3.1, 1.8, 1.6, and 1.7 percent in the June run.
insights.speaker: peterstevens
insights.so_what: An upward revision at every single horizon, including the far end, is the cleanest hawkish signal in this release and argues against aggressive long-end duration on disinflation hopes.
insights.quote: The projections for 2026, 2027, 2028, and 2029 are 3.3, 2.1, 1.8, and 1.8 percent, compared to 3.1, 1.8, 1.6, and 1.7 percent in June, respectively.
insights.locator: For core inflation, the SPF projections

insights.claim: The model expects inflation to revert toward the FOMC's long-run 2 percent goal more slowly than it did three months ago, with 2026 core PCE running at 3.3 percent — well above target.
insights.speaker: peterstevens
insights.so_what: Slower convergence from a 3.3 percent starting point means the model implies more time above target, supporting higher-for-longer real rate pricing.
insights.quote: the model now expects inflation to revert toward the FOMC’s long-run goal of 2 percent more slowly than it did in June
insights.locator: For core inflation, the SPF projections

insights.claim: Lower total factor productivity growth is named as a direct cause of the higher inflation path, linking the supply-side downgrade to the stickier price forecast.
insights.speaker: peterstevens
insights.so_what: This is stagflationary in structure — weaker growth and firmer inflation from the same TFP assumption — the worst combination for a rate-cut trade.
insights.quote: in part because lower TFP growth results in higher inflation
insights.locator: For core inflation, the SPF projections

insights.claim: Despite the upward revision to the mean path, SPF projections for 2026:Q3 core inflation were broadly in line with what the DSGE model had forecast in June, meaning the inflation revision is not driven by a near-term data surprise.
insights.speaker: peterstevens
insights.so_what: The inflation upgrade comes from model structure (TFP) rather than incoming prints, so it will not be validated or falsified by the next CPI/PCE release.
insights.quote: the SPF projections for 2026:Q3 were broadly in line with the DSGE forecast in June
insights.locator: For core inflation, the SPF projections

insights.claim: The 68 percent band on 2026 core PCE inflation tightened to 3.0-3.7 percent from 2.5-3.7 percent, effectively removing the possibility of a sub-3 percent print for the year in the model's view.
insights.speaker: peterstevens
insights.so_what: A lower bound moving from 2.5 to 3.0 percent is a meaningful narrowing that shrinks the case for a rapid dovish repricing this year.
insights.locator: Forecast Comparison table, Core PCE inflation (Q4/Q4) row

insights.claim: The model's estimate of the short-run real natural rate of interest is 1.9 percent annualized for 2026, revised down from 2.0 percent in the June forecast.
insights.speaker: peterstevens
insights.so_what: A near-2 percent short-run r* is high by post-2008 standards and sets a demanding bar for what counts as restrictive policy today.
insights.quote: The model’s prediction for the short-run real natural rate of interest (r*) is 1.9 percent annualized for 2026, down from 2.0 percent in June.
insights.locator: The model's prediction for the short-run real natural rate

insights.claim: r* forecasts for 2027, 2028, and 2029 were revised up to 1.8, 1.4, and 1.2 percent from 1.7, 1.3, and 1.1 percent, so the near-term cut and the out-year raise move in opposite directions.
insights.speaker: peterstevens
insights.so_what: Higher out-year r* means less room for the terminal policy rate to fall than markets assuming a low neutral rate may expect — relevant for the front end of forward curves.
insights.quote: 1.8, 1.4, and 1.2 percent for 2027, 2028, and 2029, compared to 1.7, 1.3, and 1.1 percent in June, respectively
insights.locator: The r* forecasts are slightly higher than in June

insights.claim: The model still projects r* declining steadily from 1.9 percent in 2026 to 1.2 percent by 2029, a roughly 70 basis point fall in the real neutral rate over three years.
insights.speaker: peterstevens
insights.so_what: A declining neutral rate path supports steepener logic over time but also implies today's policy stance becomes passively more restrictive if nominal rates hold.
insights.locator: Forecast Comparison table, Real natural rate of interest (Q4) row

insights.claim: The 68 percent band on r* spans roughly 0.7 to 3.1 percent for 2026 and turns negative at the lower bound by 2028 (-0.1) and 2029 (-0.5), showing the neutral rate is estimated with very low precision.
insights.speaker: peterstevens
insights.so_what: Anyone anchoring a rate view on a specific r* level is relying on a statistic whose own confidence interval spans more than two percentage points.
insights.locator: Forecast Comparison table, Real natural rate of interest (Q4) row

insights.claim: The forecast uses hard data only through 2026:Q2 and fills 2026:Q3 with external inputs — SPF median forecasts for real GDP growth and core PCE inflation, SPF short-run inflation expectations, and fed funds path expectations from the July New York Fed Survey of Market Expectations.
insights.speaker: peterstevens
insights.so_what: The current-quarter numbers are partly survey consensus rather than independent model output, so the DSGE run is not a fully independent signal for Q3.
insights.quote: The forecasts are obtained using data released through 2026:Q2, augmented for 2026:Q3 with the median forecasts for real GDP growth and core PCE inflation
insights.locator: The forecasts are obtained using data released through 2026:Q2

insights.claim: Yields on 10-year Treasury securities and Baa-rated corporate bonds are direct inputs to the model, which is the channel through which buoyant financial conditions flow into its growth estimates.
insights.speaker: peterstevens
insights.so_what: Watch Baa spreads and 10-year yields as the leading inputs that will mechanically move the next DSGE run's growth forecast.
insights.quote: as well as the yields on 10-year Treasury securities and Baa-rated corporate bonds
insights.locator: The forecasts are obtained using data released through 2026:Q2

insights.claim: The authors explicitly disclaim that the DSGE output is not an official New York Fed forecast but only one input to the Research staff's overall forecasting process.
insights.speaker: peterstevens
entities: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
insights.so_what: Do not read the 0.1 percent 2027 growth number as the New York Fed's institutional view or as a signal about the FOMC reaction function.
insights.quote: The DSGE model forecast is not an official New York Fed forecast, but only an input to the Research staff’s overall forecasting process.
insights.locator: Note: The DSGE model forecast is not an official
